Peter Giovacchini M.D.

Peter Giovacchini  

Introductory Perspectives

TODAY THE ACKNOWLEDGMENT AND discussion of countertransference responses has become respectable. This is in sharp contrast to the analytic ideology of even just a short decade back. Freud (1910) had warned us about the need to do away with our feelings toward patients since they interfered with analytic neutrality and would inevitably disrupt the course of analysis. Perhaps the analyst would have to seek further analysis for himself to achieve this objective.

With the increasing realization that analysis is a very personal experience for the analyst as well as the patient, it was concluded that the analyst's feelings cannot be swept away, nor should they be, by further training analysis. We have learned also that much can be learned about the patient through our countertransference responses (see Epstein and Feiner 1979). Indeed, in many instances, and this is especially true of patients suffering from relative fixations on primitive mental states, a favorable turn of events which preserves the analytic setting from chaotic collapse may well depend upon the recognition of how a relationship based upon the interaction of transference and countertransference elements recapitulates the repetition compulsion.

Thus, countertransference can be both good and bad for analytic resolution. Obviously, if it is unrecognized, the analyst will lose his analytic orientation, and as Freud (1910) insisted, it will lead to deleterious effects. In To Have or to Be he quotes Meister Eckhart: "Love has to do with desire and purpose, whereas knowledge is no particular thought, but rather it peels off all (coverings) and is disinterested and runs naked to God, until it touches him and grasps him." ERICH FROMM WAS THE MOST FULLY alive and awake man I have ever met or can imagine. These qualities were contagious. To be truly with him one felt fully alive and awake.

As a teenager in 1941, I had read his book, Escape From Freedom, and I found an orientation to Man and Life. The book also helped explain the barbaric holocaust we had all witnessed, and how the sadist needed the masochist, as much as the reverse, to achieve what Fromm, way back then, called "symbiosis." I was determined to leave Canada and study with this man at the White Institute. To my shock, in 1951, I found he had moved to Mexico. But this cloud had a silver lining: he would then come back to New York City 3–4 months each year and I arranged to work with him in intensive supervision—two hour sessions, four times a week for four years.

If I ask why the supervision with Fromm would lift my spirits so high, it has undoubtedly to do with the fact that Fromm saw each supervisory and analytic session as a dramatic search for truth. He was above all a truth-seeker who knew that an essential part of an analysis was to shed sham and illusion.

Earl Witenberg M.D.

Earl Witenberg

Earl G. Witenberg, M.D., Director
W.A.W. INSTITUTE
NEW YORK, NEW YORK.

Earl Witenberg  

THE WILLIAM ALANSON WHITE INSTITUTE OWES MUCH to Erich Fromm; it is fitting at this time to have an issue of Contemporary Psychoanalysis dedicated to his memory. He was one of the founders of the Institute and was its first Chairman of the Faculty (1943–49). He was instrumental in founding the "Low Cost Psychoanalytic Service" in 1948. He taught regularly at the Institute for many years after his move to Mexico in 1949. Among its senior members will be found analysands, supervisees, and students of Erich Fromm. His heritage lives in them. He will be remembered for the incisiveness of his observations—both clinical and theoretical. He was clear and direct in his formulations. He could illuminate the deepest aspects of a patient's difficulty with a formulation both confronting and comforting. Always lively, he suffered no sham or pretense. No one left an encounter with Fromm feeling "so-so"; instead admiration, delight, anger, and anxiety were the feelings engendered by him. Always concentrating on what was being said to him, he was not overly serious and had a lively sense of humor; he managed to be both warm and reserved.

Ralph Crowley M.D.

Ralph Crowley

Ralph M. Crowley, M.D.
NEW YORK, NEW YORK.

Ralph Crowley  

ERICH FROMM'S MOST IMPORTANT CONTRIBUTION to my personal and professional life was involving me in being a citizen of the world, a member of the wider and more universal human community, as he was. This he did for me through his writing, through the many courses I took with him as a graduate psychoanalyst, through my association with him on the faculty of the William Alanson White Institute when he was chairman, and through a year of personal supervision with him in 1946–1947. Just as he was student of the human condition all of his life, so I have found my satisfaction in so being.

My acquaintance with Erich was through his first work translated into English, Escape from Freedom, a poor translation for the German title, Furcht vor Freiheit, which means fear of freedom, which the book is really about. Clara Thompson had recommended this book to me. Much of what I had learned about people was in general and theoretical terms; this volume and Fromm's Man for Himself were most useful in helping me to put his ideas in formulations for patients which surprised them and helped them grow. His discussion of character types and their origin and function made much more sense to me than the Freudian accounts of character.

Edward Tauber M.D.

Edward Tauber

Edward S. Tauber, M.D.
NEW YORK, NEW YORK.

Edward Tauber  

I FIRST MET ERICH SOME 40 YEARS ago. He was easily friendly and warm and reserved. There was a gentle enthusiasm and liveliness in his manner—nothing forced, yet his amiability was evident.

Erich approached therapeutic intervention with a hopefulness and vitality that was new. His formulations were pointed and vigorous. He never missed an opportunity to see what was alive in the patient, yet not overlooking the trends that bespoke negation.

Fromm was a modest person; his forthrightness was not judgmental. He was deeply appreciative of wisdom and without being given to hero worship. In a curious way, though, he approached formidable scholarship in alien areas with unflustered confidence that was both startling and touching. He believed that intelligent genuine people could master the essence of subject matter, no matter how abstruse if properly presented. One must recognize that Fromm came out of a committed Socialist tradition which bespoke an optimistic conviction in man's capacity to search for and discover important human truths. Whatever the shortcoming, this generosity and faith in man's potential to learn and broaden his wisdom served as an inspiration and incitement for others to enter into life experience.

Fromm captured the wisdom of Buddhist thought and with Suzuki and de Martino wrote one of his finest books, "Psychoanalysis and Zen Buddism, " in which he clarified much of what seemed incomprehensible and contradictory. His profound respect for Eastern thought enriched his sense of man's search for wisdom. Yet, Fromm did not have to 'become' a Zen Buddhist. The challenge to growth is not enhanced by idolatrous worship nor cynical dismissal.

Dr. Fromm's interest in social issues began in his youth—historical, ethical and religious themes centering on man were the hallmark of his thinking. These topics were not exclusively academically focussed. Where possible, he applied himself conscientiously to taking action. It is not well known that he made numerous and often effective efforts to assist certain persons in being released from Iron Curtain countries. He made himself actively available to those who sought his advice and support in political areas where he believed humanistic motives existed.

Maurice Green M.D.

Maurice Green

Maurice R. Green, M.D.
275 Central Park West

Maurice Green  

Ullman, M., M.D. and Zimmerman, N. Working with Dreams. New York: Delacorte Press, 1979.

IT IS WITH GREAT PLEASURE that I commend this book by Monty Ullman, and his co-author, Nan Zimmerman. It is a refreshingly clear and readable book, readily understood by the average person with none of the jargon that has characterized and obscured so much in this area.

I have participated in a professional group workshop with Monty for many years, and more recently in a lay group meeting that is well captured by this book.

He begins with the common questions that have been asked of psychoanalysts over and over again, particularly by lay people. However, the questions, along with the responses expressed in very simple language, manifest a high degree of expert knowledge. His purpose is to inform the community of this knowledge, and encourage "non-experts" to develop skill and pleasure in the use of and the sharing of dreams.

His second chapter on the history of the use of dreams repeats some of what has been said in the many previous histories and adds a great deal that is fresh and enlivening.

His brief chapter on Freud's approach to the use of the dream expresses his deep respect for Freud's important contribution as one among many. He also briefly does justice to Jung's important work and presents a neat little table summarizing three approaches—Freud's, Jung's and Ullmann's.

He presents the laboratory research on sleep that is least technical and most relevant to a popular understanding with no pretense at an authoritative summary. However, it is nonetheless reflective of his thorough familiarity with the research data. His use of diagrams make this even more readily available.

To the Editor

I'M WRITING THIS NOTE in response to Dr. Edgar A. Levenson's smooth updating of the premises which should inform the structure of psychoanalytic thinking (Contemporary Psychoanalysis, 16:1–15). I find much in his paper with which I agree—my own view is interactive, relational. But I wish to voice what seems to be an important caution.

First, I'm not sure that a relational epistemology must or should exclude a "depth" image. Dr. Levenson is opposed to reducing surface phenomena to depth genotypes. He associates the "depth" metaphor with mechanistic thinking which turns appearances into epiphenomena, and so argues against the necessity or desirability of the "depth" category. I, also, am reluctant to reduce relational presences to something "behind" them—but this in itself doesn't make the depth dimension superfluous.

I wish to argue that depth is a radically important quality of human experience, a well nigh universal structure (especially among all "higher" civilizations), like it or not. It represents a dimension of experience far more general than the mechanistic, and cannot be derived from the latter. Mechanistic meanings or uses of depth notions in science, philosophy or everyday life constitute only a contracted form this category of experience may take, albeit a potentially devastating one.

Max Deutscher 1916-1979

John Schimel M.D.

John Schimel

John Schimel  

MAX DEUTSCHER EXEMPLIFIED THE spirit of the William Alanson White Psychoanalytic Institute for more than 30 years, from the time he first became a candidate. It now seems natural that he would matriculate at an institute known for its interpersonal view of psychoanalysis and of life and living generally. I believe that Max was born with a special talent for the interpersonal in living among his fellows. Naturally outgoing, with an unusual capacity for warmth and spontaneity, Max was a lively and gifted participant in the classes he attended as a candidate. Seminars taken with Max were never dull. His willingness to speak up, take a chance, and his lively and probing intelligence invariably stimulated exhilarating discussions into which shyer peers were regularly drawn. Even then, Max's sensitive understanding of patients and his delicacy in his dealings with them were admired and envied by fellow candidates. He learned quickly and perceptively, showing a keen sense of discrimination in being able to sort out the wheat from the chaff in the immense amount of information offered in the Institute's curriculum. He was an omnivorous reader with an excellent memory and the ability to synthesize rapidly, fluently and persuasively, bits and pieces from his reading, clinical and other living experiences.

Max had distinguished himself before enrolling at the Institute. He had rendered meritorious service to the Navy in the Pacific Theatre during World War II. He had participated in the research upon which the Supreme Court of the United States based its verdict in Brown vs. Brown, which struck down the discriminatory separate-but-equal education doctrine. Max had been pleased to have been part of this important work. He came to the Institute to share in the new, exciting and humanistic understanding of people that was being developed by Erich Fromm, Frieda Fromm-Reichmann, Harry Stack Sullivan, Clara Thompson, Janet and David Rioch, and others.

From Notes for a paper on anniversary reactions involving abortions

I DEVELOPED SOME VIEW of these anniversary experiences as denied traumas of adult life, of an exceptional and unusual type. I think at that time I had not as yet integrated a point of view of the significance of the separation-individuation cycles over the course of the life cycle, and of the kinds of transitional experiences that life had, the recycling course of living, the notion of mourning and incomplete mourning that was involved in transitions into autonomy. From an autobiographical point of view, I was a new father, more related to babies and mothers and wives and the immediate pleasures and stresses, than with the long overview of the course and processes of living. ERICH FROMM WAS BORN IN Frankfurt a.m. Germany on March 23, 1900. On the father's side, there has been a long rabbinical tradition and Fromm had an opportunity to familiarize himself with the teachings of the Talmud since his childhood.

The concepts of the Old Testament, the radical humanism of Karl Marx, and the pessimistically tinged psychoanalytic discoveries of Freud represent cornerstones in Fromm's concept of man. His academic background was in the field of psychology, sociology and philosophy. Fromm obtained his Ph.D. at the University of Heidelberg at the age of twenty-two. He went for further studies to the University of Munich, and later on, moved to Berlin where he became a member of the Berlin Psychoanalytic Institute. His training analysis was with Hans Sachs and he was graduated from the Berlin Psychoanalytic Institute in 1931. The Psychoanalytic Institute in Frankfurt, Germany was co-founded by Fromm and Frieda Fromm-Reichmann.

Fromm received an invitation from Franz Alexander to join the Chicago Psychoanalytic Institute and came to the United States in 1933. About a year later he moved to New York City where he assumed an active role as a teacher, practicing analyst and writer. He was among a small group of psychoanalysts who founded the William Alanson White Institute in New York whose director was Clara Thompson. Later Fromm moved to Bennington where he taught and practiced while maintaining his association with the William Alanson White Institute.

FOR MAX DEUTSCHER [1916–1979], co-Founding Editor of Contemporary Psychoanalysis, each issue is a tribute. In this journal we shall express the thinking and experience of the professional community bearing on psychoanalytic issues.

Psychoanalysis is in the midst of challenge and growth which it shares with the other sciences and humanities, with present-day society itself.

… we hope that Contemporary Psychoanalysis will become a significant forum for the psychoanalytic community.

SUMMARY

Alicia took leave from her family in a hostile manner. Presumably she also left the analyst with a good deal of resentment because she had aroused what Alicia had so long tried to lull to sleep with "Peace, Peace, Peace."

What had the analyst done? Through the interpretation of two dreams, she had brought to Alicia's awareness the nature of her

101

relationships with people; the meaning of her evasiveness; the meaning of her derealization, of her indifference and detachment, of her joy in surrender, the meaning of her feeling a complete stranger in New York and of crossing out her past. Most important, the analyst brought her to an awareness of her "bad me," implying that she did not really believe in her "good me" because it had been imposed on her. The analyst pointed out her deeply hidden disappointment and resentment, which went together with the "bad me," and made her previously dissociated hostility and anger real for her.

These insights must have made her angry, and it must have made her angry, too, that her mask was torn down. Yet during the sessions with the analyst, she seemed very receptive, repeating often, "Believe me, I understand you, everything makes sense to me, I am so grateful you told me this, so glad I came to see you," and, a few times, "But what can I do?" The same tone prevailed her last morning in New York when we spoke for another fifteen minutes on the phone.

She left aloof, detached, and completely disinterested in her family, which had shown real warmth and concern for her. The change in behavior toward her stepmother and the brother was striking. Where she had been cordial and playful with them, now she could no longer act her role. The mask had fallen down, and she had been confronted with her inner reality.

I wish to describe a particular phase of my experience with him because it remained for me the most unforgettable thing that happened between us. It belongs on the record as a fact about his work that often escapes the notice it deserves. As a direct reflection of the system of beliefs, values, and ideals presumably shot through our success-oriented culture, we are too deeply conditioned to look for the so-called bottom line—that is to say, for the product rather than the process, or for the goal rather than the path.

THERE IS, IN TRUTH, STILL NO ROYAL ROAD to the makings of psychoanalytic self-knowledge. It is not at all like the status acquired by familial, cultural, or social inheritance; it is far more like a way station along a disciplined, caring, and deeply vital journey within. And now: the quest for any such royal road obviously a failure; the promise either of biology or of sociology, or of both together, to pave that road no longer rational; a psychology of self-knowledge guaranteed by the sciences external to its experience but a pleasant dream of yesteryear's enlightenment. A psychology of self-knowledge, it is becoming increasingly clear, may be reached only through the direct psychic effort of the individual who seeks it—first-personal, singular, active, and fundamentally original—that is to say, necessarily originating—from within the resourceful conditions of that individual's own uniqueness.

Darlene Ehrenberg Ph.D. and Arthur Feiner Ph.D.

Arthur Feiner

Arthur Feiner  

THIS ISSUE OF CONTEMPORARY PSYCHOANALYSIS is dedicated to the memory of Erich Fromm, one of the founders of the William Alanson White Institute. He was a pioneer in psychoanalysis, focusing his attention on the interaction among intrapsychic, interpersonal and social forces. He went far beyond the orthodoxy of his early training though he considered himself a Freudian until the end. His passionate humanism, which brought him into close contact with Harry Stack Sullivan and Clara Thompson, was an inspiration for many of us. His interest in authenticity in presence, one's sensitivity to one's own feelings as antidote to alienation, his focus on analytic data as reflective of social attitudes and social practice, and indications of the actual way lives were lived, and his emphasis on the dialectic in interpretation were brilliant beacons in a foggy atmosphere. Like all stimulating teachers, those who draw out of us the best we can do, Dr. Fromm was of many facets. His commitment to social humanism, seemed in later years, to have greater priority for him, over his seminal interests in the psychoanalytic process. Our focus, of course, in this Journal, is on psychoanalytic theory and technique. It is in his courageous, pioneering spirit, his assertion of the value of growth and openness to change, that we have gathered this collection of tributes, commentaries and original essays, dedicated to his memory.

Anna Gourevitch
NEW YORK, NEW YORK.

Anna Gourevitch  

I MET ERICH FROMM IN 1943 half a year after my arrival in the United States, as a result of my fourteen year old son giving me Escape from Freedom. Reading this book made me determined to study with Fromm. He was teaching at that time at the Washington School of Psychiatry in the Murray Hill Hotel. The lectures were fascinating and I approached Erich after one of them, wanting to clarify certain aspects of his comments. We pursued the conversation for hours and the tone of the friendship that was established that evening lasted for years. For him, friendship included the sharing of common interests, deep loyalty and also humor. At the end of our first conversation, Erich suggested another meeting the following Friday, but as he stressed, "Five o'clock American time, not Russian time." Whatever the topic we touched upon over the years, we explored its full meaning and importance to us, picking up where we left off at our last meeting, so that his move to Mexico later did not interfere with the continuity of our relationship.

I had been sharing some of Erich's opinions before I met him. Both of us had been trying to come to terms with certain problems concerning psychoanalysis, particularly the conventionality in the orthodox approach and the replacement of the effort to understand the world of the patient with stereotyped interpretations. The problem of the absence of a live approach was familiar to me and I was happy that he could express the total concept of his thinking about this so well and convincingly, things that few people had touched upon previously. Let me quote his own words from an interview from the German newspaper Die Zeit, March 21, 1980:

As a student, I remained a good Freudian. True, my doubts increased but I graduated from the very orthodox Berlin Psychoanalytic Institute … and during the following five or six years, my analyses adhered strictly to what I had learned. I expected to hear from the patient that which was in accordance with the theory. … I finally realized that everything turned out to be as I expected it, never anything new, always well defined conceptions: the Oedipus complex, fear of castration and so on.

came with that curious sense of shock that long-delayed expectation evokes.

With Death comes the reintegration of the perception and image of the other person, that for a while seems larger than life, but actually is life; is that person. For once, the fragmented perceptions become the Whole, and that truly is greater than the sum of its parts. Is this the experience that primitives have spoken of as the spirit hovering over the body it has left; is it the projection of the synthesis?

Fromm in a very singular way is woven into my Self. He has been and now more than ever is a presence for me which Death sharpens. "Erich, " (I wrote to Annis1), "is a friend in the most profound sense, my teacher to whom I turned thirstily for nurturing the Self that was nascent within me. He provided for me missing pieces that I was seeking 'out there, '" (though I am indebted to many).

I became acquainted with him stimulated through Clara's2 description of him and his interests, his courage and achievement. I began following him about to the courses he gave at the New School and to analysts-in-training, before the separation of the White Institute-to-be from the Horney group, which in fact occurred because of the issue of his not being an M.D. and giving clinical rather than theoretical courses. Then he became supervisor, analyst, colleague, and friend to me. At times, I travelled to Bennington, and Mexico for analysis, and then to teach, at the newly founded psychoanalytic institute in Mexico. I later visited him in Europe and here and there, and as friendship developed, met with his wife Henny in Mexico, who died suddenly, and then with Annis.

IN THIS ESSAY I WOULD LIKE to look at Paul Ricoeur's conception of the status of psychoanalysis as a science (Ricoeur 1977), but to look at his argument in the context of intersubjective recognition, what intersubjectivity implies for understanding the symbol-productions of schizophrenic language, and what the scientific claims of psychoanalysis reveal about the origin of psychic facts and their representation in language. It should be added that much of what Ricoeur argues about truth claims in psychoanalysis, the nature of communication, intersubjectivity, the status of psychic facts (the productions of the inner), and the significance of symbolic language, reflect directions in the writings of Harry Stack Sullivan. It would of course require a considerably more detailed analysis than is possible here to do justice to the full range of thematic parallels. Yet similarities do exist, and I shall on occasion note a few of them.

CHARLES DARWIN ONCE CLASSIFIED SCIENTISTS as either "splitters" or "lumpers." Erich Fromm, who died at the age of 79 in Lucerne, Switzerland, on March 18, 1980, was clearly a lumper. Trained as a psychoanalyst, Fromm emerged, on the basis of his own erudition, as a social critic and moral philosopher of considerable reknown. In a very real sense he applied his gifts as a clinician to diagnoses of the ills of society and of social institutions. His well-known books such as Escape From Freedom, The Sane Society, and The Art of Loving attest not only to his original social insights but also to his ability to communicate his ideas simply and directly to a wide audience.

Erich Fromm was born in Germany in 1900 to middle-class Jewish parents. After completing his work at the Gymnasium, he attended the University of Heidelberg, where he studied sociology, philosophy, and psychology, attaining his Ph.D. at the age of 22. Although Fromm's scholarly interests were deep and abiding, so too was his concern for people; this concern stimulated his interest in psychoanalysis. At that time (in accord with Freud's wishes) the training of lay analysts was common practice, and Fromm was accepted and trained at the Berlin Psychoanalytic Institute.

At the Berlin Institute Fromm met and married his first wife, Freida Fromm-Reichmann. After completing their training, Fromm and his wife helped to found and run the Psychoanalytic Institute in Frankfurt. In 1933, as the political situation in Germany worsened, Fromm accepted an invitation from the Chicago Psychoanalytic Institute to come to the United States. Fromm liked America, but preferring to settle in New York City instead of Chicago, he became one of the founders and trustees, along with Harry Stack Sullivan, of the William Alanson White Institute.

THIS PAPER ATTEMPTS TO SUMMARIZE a series of twelve lectures on Nietzsche, given twice at Loyola University of Chicago in the fall and winter semesters 1980-1981. Following Nietzsche's provocative style, I have utilized a form which I think Nietzsche would have approved of and which, like his famous German rhetoric, I hope also best illustrates his basic philosophy.

Presentation

Every achievement of knowledge is a consequence of courage, of severity toward oneself, of cleanliness toward oneself … to wash one's soul ever cleaner from the marketplace dust and noise of this age.

Nietzsche, The Will to Power (1968, pp. 536 and 541)

I, FRIEDRICH NIETZSCHE, WAS BORN in a small town in Prussia in 1844 to a 31 year old Lutheran minister father and the daughter of another Lutheran minister; she was only 18. I was their first child. Two years later, in 1846, my "demonic" (Kaufmann 1968) sister Elizabeth was born; in two more years, 1848, my brother Joseph was born. When I was five years old, in 1849, my father died of madness—probably general paresis, and in January, 1850, Joseph died (Fuss and Shapiro 1971).

As I wrote, I became after that time a homeless wanderer obsessively seeking what I called the shadow of God (Nietzsche 1968a), (Copleston 1975).

THERE IS A SPECIAL RELATIONSHIP between man and wife during pregnancy because of what they have to accomplish during that period. United in their goal, they nevertheless have different biological tasks. These differences give rise to individual communication styles. The woman feels and expresses her bodily changes directly; the man expresses his experience indirectly through empathy and perceptions which vary from the conscious to the subliminal. It is in part the response to the body changes of pregnancy that early identifications emerge from repression, allowing for their reinstatement in consciousness. Once in consciousness, they can then be worked through.

The biological accomodations which women must make during pregnancy are meaningful to the extent that they experience themselves creating a new person conceived in love of the man and immortalizing themselves and that love through the birth and care of the child. It is the emotional goal of pregnancy to conclude it with the family of man—father-mother-child. In pursuit of this, however far she wanders, the woman must come home to the man, for she needs this relationship for her mothering to be mature. As has been amply documented, during their pregnancy women identify with their mothers in mothering, review their dependencies and try out a variety of roles of the child-mother type, play-acting in fantasy and reality the various possibilities of caring and being cared for.

In order to rehearse for her part, the woman must withdraw part of her care and concern from her husband. Yet, she must be able to depend on his presence as a protector, provider and intimate.

Anna Gourevitch  

IN SUCCESSFUL ANALYSIS, THE patient will discover the elements of his unconscious that interfere with his self-realization and learn to integrate them into his personality. These acquired insights should be liberating, freeing at least some of the energy bound by the protective and defensive neurotic systems. Eventually they should allow the person to see himself and his present life-situation more objectively, and help him be more responsive to the surrounding world. Little by little the general confusion and undifferentiated notions about the world and people will subside, ordered by a new understanding of the neurotic structure and its defensive patterns of behavior.

Not all of the people who enter our offices are willing to change. In fact, more commonly they want to change reality and not themselves. Real change, the result of confrontation with oneself and one's life, seems terrifying, and the ego-strength necessary to face their emotional turbulence, their nameless fears and self-doubts is often not available. So they stay prisoners of the fictitious balance they have created. The problem, however (which their discomfort signals), is that the precarious harmony is an illusion and not a genuine achievement. Its cost is the repression of all inner conflicts and feelings, which consumes energy and produces anxiety and tension. It also permanently eliminates the possibility of commitment to and involvement with the world and the Other.

Ralph, an engineer who came to see me in his early forties, is typical. His older brother, a renowned Ivy League professor, was clearly a decisive figure in his life, although Ralph only mentioned that he did not know him well. In fact, his brother had been a decisive identification figure when Ralph was a teenager, whom he had looked up to for the acceptance and guidance that could not come from a detached father and epileptic mother. However, the brother was preoccupied with his own career and tolerated Ralph only so long as he did not make any real demands.

Ruth Imber Ph.D.

Ruth Imber

Ruth Imber, Ph.D.
390 West End Avenue
New York, New York 10024

Ruth Imber  

Leon Salzman, M.D., Treatment of the Obsessive Personality.

New York: Jason Aronson, Inc.

THE PSYCHODYNAMICS OF THE OBSESSIONAL neurosis have been studied and explicated quite thoroughly since Freud's presentation of the Rat Man. Both the typical symptomotology and predominant defense mechanisms employed have been spelled out methodically. Along with the hysterical neurosis it has been seen traditionally as amenable to psychoanalytic treatment, requiring little or no variation in classical technique. Yet, despite all our knowledge and experience with this diagnostic category there is a good deal of pessimism among analysts about achieving a successful outcome when working with an obsessional. "Clinically speaking … it cannot be denied that a major obsessional neurosis is a severe and intractable disorder in which only moderate analytical accessibility prevails." (Glover 1955, p. 205). Why should this be so? Why should work with these patients often be considered laborious, tedious and boring?

Various explanations can be offered. Fenichel (1945) systematically lists several difficulties which he sees as idiosyncratic to the obsessional neurosis. For instance, free association or compliance with "the basic rule" is almost impossible because the patient is always unconsciously censoring irrational thoughts and impulses while striving to be reasonable. The rigid avoidance of emotional experience and a tendency to intellectualize can lead to much talk for talk's sake. Also, the positive value which our culture places on qualities such as punctuality, cleanliness, orderliness, etc. furnishes secondary gains which compound the work of exposing defensive functioning.

IN PREINDUSTRIAL SOCIETIES WHERE THERE is no television, radio, literature or formal schooling, stories and myths play a crucial role in shaping the developmental process. It is difficult for Westerners to appreciate how important folklore can be in interpreting the world to a child, in defining the emotional ties with caretakers, and in providing a shared symbolic language familar to all. Originally intending to study personality development among the Apache, Bryce Boyer was led to his concern with the importance of Apache folklore through his original and creative research method: for periods of as long as fifteen months, over many years, Boyer served as psychiatrist to the Apache, living on the reservation, studying resistances and transference reactions and their implications. As a highly experienced and astute clinician (he has contributed to the pages of this Journal), he has been able to create a picture of Apache personality through observing reactions to interpretations in the treatment process. In the course of this work, he found that the Apache often made overt or veiled references to folklore, and reared their children in the constant awareness of mythic figures, mountain spirits, ghosts and witches. For example, toddlers are typically threatened with the whippoorwill who is believed to become a cannibal woman at night who will carry off a crying child if it doesn't stop bothering a parent. In this way the folklore serves as a displacement system—children learn to direct their fear and anger onto culturally provided figures, as parents express their hostility through the "bogeyman". PSYCHOANALYTIC TREATMENT IS CARRIED OUT in the context of the transference regression. Whatever extensions or modifications may occur in the theoretical edifice, the method remains essentially the same. What we interpret may vary, but our main technical approach is the interpretation of the transference; this may be considered an invariant. What we interpret, however, is not invariant. Our interpretations will be determined by how we understand the patient's associations and reactions as they lie on our couches, and this has changed in the last two decades. This is where early object relationships and psychic development enter the picture.

Freud (1912) stressed how the analyst, as a clinician, has to suspend judgments, abandon preconceived formulations and follow the patient's associations wherever they may lead. Some analysts who have been analyzed by him indicate that Freud did not practice what he preached. Instead, he tried to make everything fit into the Oedipal mold. Holt (1973) demonstrated Freud's propensity to generalize from very small bits of data. His devotion to the death instinct and his insistence on the universality of the Oedipus complex are two noteworthy examples that have had a tremendous influence on the practice of psychoanalysis. For example, the death instinct, as it has been absorbed in the Kleinian model, has become the foundation for the interpretations of a large group of analysts, particularly those living south of the border, extending from Mexico to Argentina. THE MUTUAL INSENSITIVITIES of interpersonal and object relations theories to each other are remarkable. Not so remarkable, perhaps, if one keeps in mind Witenberg's (1976) comments about dogma and the "need to believe" in the face of uncertainty.

Psychoanalytic politics can be likened to religious sectarianism. Belief systems tend to atrophy into self-perpetuating dogmas. Karl Mannheim's (1936) speculations on the sociology of knowledge are germane. He indicates how "ideologies" function to stabilize a social order. Both "churches"—interpersonal and object relations—have perhaps needed to hold to ideologies built on selective inattention to differeing beliefs. Dialectical exchanges between the "churches" are hindered by pre-syntactic experiences, each of the other.

In the context of rapid growth of possibilities and technologies for international scientific communication, little exchange goes on. American psychoanalysis has been relatively impervious to the penetration of the "English school." This speaks to a primitive xenophobia which needs to preserve its ideologies.

Erikson has called this global fragmentation of the human species "pseudospeciation." "Pseudospeciation" grows from the need to be "in" by making others "out, " to exaggerate one's plumage to escape from the nakedness of being simply more human than otherwise. Erikson's concept addresses how "while man is obviously one species, he appears and continues on earth split up into groups … which provide their members with a firm sense of God-given identity—and a sense of immortality" (Erikson 1975, p. 176).

IN THIS ESSAY, I DO the following: first, I differentiate those characteristics of the borderline and the narcissistic personality organizations which, I believe, contribute to important variations in the transference-countertransference matrices typically established by one and the other type of patient. This will include comments on the Kernberg-Kohut controversy. Secondly, I consider how the countertransference difficulties generated by the massive resistances of the borderline patient might induce psychoanalysts to disqualify such patients as analyzable, or to otherwise mistreat them.1

In responding to an earlier draft of this paper, some colleagues challenged the premise that persons can be meaningfully differentiated into one or another of such personality organizations, raising larger issues concerning the pitfalls of diagnostic labeling.2 Once we pin a label on a person, or accept a label as given—and this can begin, of course, with the label, 'patient'—we may be led easily to think of the person as some-thing-known. And, this may stimulate in our thoughts, a process which begins with depriving the patient of his personhood and ends by negating his therapeutic need to be understood as fully as possible in his own terms.

ALTHOUGH ERICH FROMM PUBLISHED 22 books and nearly 100 articles on psychoanalysis and related matters, he wrote little specifically on technique. He long planned to do so and had begun to write on this topic just before his death in 1980. He waited, I believe, because he felt that too strong a focus on methodology would not do justice to the vital spirit of the therapeutic engagement. At the same time, perhaps paradoxically, Fromm insisted that sound methodology was necessary for effective inquiry because of the complexity of the transactions; he strongly believed that there was a science of psychoanalysis and he taught this for some fifty years in seminars and supervision. It was my privilege to have studied with Erich Fromm and, later on, to know him in a more personal way; this paper is based on my own understanding and experience of the principles of psychoanalytic practice that Erich Fromm developed.

Although the analytic relationship by itself is not curative, since a psychoanalytic cure is based on overcoming repression and the distortions that arise from it, the establishment of a "productive relatedness" is primary in Fromm's approach to psychoanalysis.

The analyst understands the patient only inasmuch as he experiences in himself all that the patient experiences; otherwise he will have only intellectual knowledge about the patient, but will never really know what the patient experiences, nor will he be able to convey to him that he shares and understands his (the patient's) experience. WE HAVE BEEN ATTEMPTING in a series of studies to transpose the central theoretical ideas of Freudian psychoanalysis into a metapsychology-free framework, a "psychoanalytic phenomenology, " which takes the representational world (Sandler & Rosenblatt 1962) as its principal construct and focus. These studies have been guided by the dual aim of preserving and clarifying and clarifying the seminal clinical insights embedded in (and frequently obscured by) classical metapsychology, and of recasting them in a form which makes possible an articulation and integration of the psychoanalytic system with other theoretical points of view.

To these ends, we have proposed that the following components constitute the necessary and sufficient ingredients for a clinically meaningful psychoanalytic psychology of the representational world: (1) the distinctive configurations of self and object which can be shown to pervade a person's experiences; (2) the developmental tasks (for example, differentiation and integration) which a developing person must negotiate in order to articulate and consolidate his representational world; and (3) the various conscious and unconscious purposes (for example, wish-fulfilling, self-guiding and self-punishing, adaptive, restitutive-reparative, and defensive purposes) that may be served by the representational configurations which are established in the course of a person's life cycle.

As distinct from metapsychology, psychoanalytic phenomenology does not postualate a theory of the nature of personality as an objective entity. Instead, it consists in a methodological system of interpretive principles to guide the study of meaning in human experience and conduct. As such, it aims to elucidate the nature, developmental vicissitudes, functional significance, and therapeutic transformations of the representational structures that permeate and unconsciously organize a person's subjective world.

IN THE FOURTH CENTURY B.C. a Taoist monk, Chuang Tsu, wrote a now famous parable:

Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tsu, dreamed I was a butterfly, flying happily here and there. Suddenly I woke up and I was indeed Chuang Tsu. Did Chuang Tsu dream he was the butterfly, or did the butterfly dream he was Chuang Tsu? (Feng & English 1974).

This may seem a rather esoteric way to start a presentation on the data of psychoanalysis, but the question is germane. Who dreams the dream? Does the dream perhaps dream the dreamer? My thesis is that it is precisely this issue which lies at the core of a major psychoanalytic schism, one with profound and perhaps irreconcilable consequences for our understanding of the process of therapy and the very nature of change, itself.

We would all agree that symbolization, in its divers manifestations (dreams, fantasies, the patient's representation of events, even language, itself), mirrors actual events. But when there is distortion, when an evident gap exists between real events and their symbolic representation, does the distortion reflect an attempt to grapple with a poorly comprehended reality; or, is the reality only a jumping-off point for an autonomous fantasy process, internally drive and motivated? It is on this point that the intra-psychic and interpersonal analysts differ most sharply.

TRADITIONAL ACCOUNTS OF PSYCHOANALYTIC PSYCHOLOGY usually emphasize the way in which crude sexual and aggressive impulses attempt to force their way towards the surface of the mind, to find expression in the individual's subjective experience and overt behaviour. On the path from the depths to the surface such impulses may be felt to be dangerous, may arouse conflict in the mind and have to be defended against or censored, distorted so that their true meaning is hidden from the person's own consciousness. Although such defensive distortion and censorship is a normal process, a consequence of the child's progressive socialization, the outcome of conflict and defence may under certain circumstances be regarded as pathological.

Within the traditional theoretical framework of psychoanalysis the persons towards whom the impulses are directed, either in fantasy or reality, are the objects of the drives—hence, of course, the term object relationships. Such object relationships have been accounted for in classical psychoanalytic theory in terms of the investment of the object (or its mental representation) with instinctual drive energy, either in its original crude state or in a neutralized, purified or sublimated form.

In contrast to the linking of psychopathology with conflict over primitive instinctual impulses, there has been an increasing tendency over the past few decades to describe and explain both normal and pathological processes in terms of the vicissitudes of the individual's object relationships. INTRODUCTION

A PERSPECTIVE ON INTERPRETIVE METAPSYCHOLOGY has, in recent years, been emerging from a specific point of view, namely, for the conduct of a unique and individual, and, in basic respects, induplicable experience of psychoanalytic therapy. It points toward the increasing acceptance of the full psychic realism of that therapeutic experience, as it actually takes place, however it may later be interpreted and speculated about. That perspective not only requires a number of primary and irreversible changes in the structure of psychoanalytic inquiry, it also reflects a number of innovative changes in the limits and possibilities of the clinical psychoanalytic picture.

In theoretical effect, those changes open the order of metapsychology, without reservation, to all the interpretive myths and metaphors held by a potentially infinite universe of psychoanalysts and patients. For practical purposes, they open the range of interpretive and speculative readings of the actual psychoanalytic experience, again without reservation, to any myth or metaphor seriously invoked by any psychoanalyst or patient in the course of a particular therapeutic inquiry. In the context of changes of such magnitude, a perspective of psychic realism, without prejudice or prejudgment, allows for the indefinitely extended differences among psychoanalysts and patients, and supports their appeal to a growing pluralism of metapsychologies.

WHAT I HAVE TO SAY IS BASED on my experience and interpretations of some years of contact with Fromm through seminars and supervision and a recent month-long conference in Mexico. I cannot help but tell you a little of this last experience since it was not only stimulating of new ideas, but was also inspiring of belief in the possibilities of analysts talking openly to one another about their personal conceptions of neurosis and therapy. Admittedly the stage for our three week case seminar was set in that rarified atmosphere of Cuernavaca with its breathtaking vista of mountains rolling out to infinity. To further enhance these ideal working conditions, the seven participants had, for 10 days, just shared an intensive experience in a conference on "Zen Buddhism and Psychoanalysis" which provoked us all to review many of the premises which underlie our work.

But of late I have been increasingly able to catch, if I listen attentively, the sound of the sobs which I had the strength to control in my father's presence, and which broke out only when I found myself alone with Mamma. Actually, their echo has never ceased: it is only because life is now growing more and more quiet round about me that I hear them afresh, like those convent bells which are so effectively drowned during the day by the noises of the streets that one would suppose them to have been stopped for ever, until they sound out again through the silent evening air.
Swann's Way, M. Proust

OBJECT RELATIONS THEORY HAS BECOME one of the ubiquitous phrases within contemporary psychoanalytic literature. It is used variously to refer to: theorists who have departed from the classical tradition, like Klein and Fairbairn; theorists who have remained within the tradition yet stretched its boundaries like Mahler, Jacobson and Kernberg; as well as to all those who acknowledge the importance that other people play in personality development. Within this spread of meaning and amid the controversies among dedicated proponents and denigrating detractors, the term "object relations theory" loses much of its significance. In fact, with its current wave of popularity, object relations theory threatens to degenerate into a tired psychoanalytic cliche, becoming for psychoanalysis what existentialism was for philosophy during the 1950's and 1960's—an innovative and powerful theoretical framework which became, in its ever widening application, thinned to simplistic truisms.

MY PURPOSE TODAY IS TO DISCUSS this year's White Society theme, the interpenetration of interpersonal and object relations theories, from the perspective of its clinical implications. My focus will be on the broadest aspect of this issue, the theory of the therapeutic action of psychoanalysis. I am going to approach the problem through a back door, by pointing to some recent ferment within classical psychoanalysis. This approach will, I hope, illuminate some of the problems which come up in any discussion of the relationship between theory and practice.

The past five or ten years have seen an unprecedented outpouring of criticism directed against Freudian metapsychology by analysts who were trained in and who have contributed to the classical tradition. The modifications which have been suggested, although they differ significantly from each other, share a common directional thrust: each represents an attempt to substitute a psychology predicated on experience and meaning for one based on structure and mechanism. "MY HEART KEEPS POUNDING AND POUNDING and I can't settle down …": a twenty-two-year-old young woman as she began to cry. Another woman, a thirty-year-old mother of a four-year-old child, abruptly sat up on the couch, saying, "I can't take any more; I've got to go." As she ran from the office, she acknowledged she was frightened, slammed shut the bathroom door, and "cried hysterically" in the dark. A man in his early forties started the hour with a sad look, saying, "I feel bad in my body too much—it's like getting an anxious feeling in the pit of my stomach when I try to avoid giving my ticket to the conductor."

In the quiet seclusion of the analytic office, all these people were suffering anxiety; they were afraid of something. I presume no one would take exception to the comment "[they] were suffering anxiety; they were afraid of something," yet this statement contains the source of unclarity, inconsistency, and confusion. A conscientious scan of the literature of fear and anxiety discloses no clear differentiation—the discussions are usually diligent, often profound and provocative, but nevertheless inconclusive (e.g. Freud 1936), (Goldstein 1963), (Arieti 1970), Sullivan 1953, (Horney 1937), (May 1977).1 Anxiety, as I view it, is fear that comes from danger to, or disruption of, the subjective sense one has while functioning, the familiar sense of me.

WHILE A PERSPECTIVE OF PSYCHIC REALISM, as suggested in the first part of this paper, has definite implications for psychoanalytic metapsychology, some of which I shall consider below, psychic realism is essentially focussed on the unique and shareable aspects of the clinical psychoanalytic inquiry. That focus points up the primary reality of the actual clinical experience, in contrast to the interpretive and speculative symbolism of the wide variety of terms and trends of metapsychology. As Freud once remarked, the unconscious is "the true psychical reality." And whether we now subscribe to his formulations of the meanings and the metaphors of unconscious psychic experience, it is, nonetheless, still the case that psychoanalysis is predominantly concerned with the empirical and the systematic study of "the true psychical reality."

Even the most radical clinical psychoanalytic empiricism, on the other hand, requires the introduction of some interpretive and speculative metapsychology. The therapeutic power of simplicity and directness in the immediacies of the psychoanalytic process is undeniable. Yet, if that power is not to be turned irrational and become self-serving, it must be bounded by the realistic and objective conditions of the inquiry.

León Grinberg M.D. and Rebeca Grinberg M.D.

Francisco Gervas 11-110, D

Rebeca Grinberg  

INTRODUCTION

WE SHALL TAKE AS THE STARTING POINT for our consideration of the nature and development of object relationships in the psychoanalytic process, the following paragraph of the prose poem by the philosopher Martin Buber (1937), "I and Thou":

The prenatal life of the child is a purely natural combination of bodily interaction and of the flowing of one into the other. When it is born, the full extent of its life appears to stem from the person who gave it its being. However, the child does not only rest, in the human mother's body. This relationship has such a cosmic quality, as the Talmudical saying "Man knows the universe inside his mother's body, but when he is born, he forgets it …" appears to be an imperfect interpretation of an inscription from the most remote times. And truly, it remains in man as a secret image of something he desires. It does not mean that this desire is a desire to return … rather it is a desire of a cosmic relationship with the true "Thou".

It is quite clear that this initial relationship of the baby with its mother plays a fundamental role in the psychobiological development of the child, and will influence all his subsequent experiences. This desire for the continued renewal of the dialogue between the "I" and the "Thou", in all its many vicissitudes, (with the inclusion or exclusion of the third person "He") will continue throughout life. It is precisely this existing dialectic or interplay between subject and object which determines the specific operational field of the psychoanalytic process. The interpretation of each event as a result of the correlation between the different moments of progress and regression which give rise to a continued development, introducing the dimension of time in the spacial and operational field of the linking process which has developed between the patient and the analyst, also corresponds to this dialectic point of view.

James Grotstein  

WILFRED RUPRECHT BION'S DEATH ON November 8, 1979 has thrust upon us the task of re-evaluating the impact he and his work have had on psychoanalysis in our generation. All those who have been in his presence, whether briefly or lengthy, swear—almost to a person—to the enormity of his vitality, to the power of his presence, to the humor of his dry wit, to the incisiveness of his thinking, and to the (sadly) anachronistic gentleness of his politeness and respect for people. His life story, such as I know of it, touches at many points onto the scroll of the Age of Heroes in which so many of our childhoods were so passionately spent vicariously. Bion may very well qualify as a modern equivalent of a classical hero, not only by virtue of his remote birth and his World War I exploits but also because of his being such a fearless champion of our Innocence (at least, for those of us who were his analysands) who grappled so handily with our dragons and enabled us to get through Blake's Forest of Experience onto the road to Higher Innocence. Yet from another perspective, one cannot read Bion's later works, particularly those which refer to the genius, the mystic, or the messiah, without applying that designation to him. What is a genius? To Bion it is one who is able to experience Truth ("O") without having to think about it (falsify it).

DR. EIGEN'S TELLING CRITIQUE of Glatzer and Evan's 1977 paper on Guntrip's personal psychoanalyses raises salient questions of clinical practice. Based on extensive conversations I had with Guntrip, I would like to comment on some of these matters. When we met in 1972, three years before his death, Guntrip was rethinking his approaches to psychoanalytic theory and engagement.

First I should like to comment on Eigen's statement that Guntrip's "major presenting symptom—a background sense of unreality—was apparently marginal, one most people would put up with or try to ignore." Guntrip did not journey seven hours north to Edinburgh for double sessions with Fairbairn, and later seven hours south to London for his meetings with Winnicott, year in and year out, because of "marginal" difficulties. The sad reality is that he felt profoundly disturbed and often endured agonizing fear, paralyzing depression and states of complete loneliness. Guntrip made no secret of this. When I remarked that his writings about the schizoid state were graphic, he replied, "Well, it's all first hand, I know what it is." He described an acute sense of feeling shut in, trapped and lifeless that was imperative to rectify.

Our meeting followed a rewarding collaboration on a writing project. He had the talent of making the other person feel warmly acknowledged for his contributions. And in person he was exceptionally considerate and generous. I had taken the train up from London and Guntrip met me at the railroad station in Leeds.

Guntrip's Analysis with Winnicott—A Critique of Glatzer and Evans

Michael Eigen Ph.D.

Michael Eigen

Michael Eigen, Ph.D.
225 Central Park West

Michael Eigen  

GUNTRIP'S (1975) ACCOUNT OF HIS PSYCHOTHERAPEUTIC journey is one of the deeply moving portrayals in analytic literature. By all usual standards he was not a clinically ill person. He functioned creatively in his work and personal life. His major presenting symptom—a background sense of unreality—was apparently marginal, one most people would put up with or try to ignore. However, he was one of those individuals who could not let any sense of "offness" rest. There was a sense in which he was not able to compromise or settle for anything less than becoming a whole person—even if this goal is necessarily elusive.

What gives Guntrip's case an added dimension is that his two analysts, Fairbairn and Winnicott, were among the most creative in the profession—and that he sensitively and creatively charted his pilgrimage. We look over his shoulder and try to catch a glimpse of who these men were and how they interacted with one another. By studying their work we must inevitably increase ourselves, even if our view is speculative and fragmentary.

Glatzer and Evans (1977) recently have raised the question "what went wrong?" in Guntrip's therapies. They feel his paper contains a veiled reproach for the shortcomings of his therapists and unconsciously portrays the lineaments of "therapeutic misalliances". (Langs 1975). Glatzer and Evans find that Guntrip's therapeutic work missed his baby hostile omnipotence and sibling rivalry. They believe that his therapists provided gratifications which masked these critical psychodynamics.

In the present paper I hope to qualify and amplify Glatzer and Evans's findings. My main interest centers on problems in Guntrip's relationship with Winnicott—Guntrip felt the stakes highest there.

MY TITLE, WITH ITS REFERENCE TO need and to desire, has an obvious connection with current discussions about the relative merits of self psychology and a more classical, analytically oriented psychology for the understanding and treatment of mental patients. The difference in approach between a self psychology and a more classical theory is often epitomized by the terms "deficit" and "conflict" rather than by "need" and "desire." Classical psychoanalysis tends to view the significant aspects of most psychopathology as secondary to unresolved conflict. Thus, someone who is phobic, inhibited or unable to sustain relationships is considered to have conflicts about his sexual wishes and about his angry reactions when his sexual wishes are frustrated. His fear or guilt about his sexual and angry feelings and fantasies leads him to repress or otherwise defend against them. However, he pays a price in that his freedom to express himself and interact with others is impaired. Treatment consists of resolving the conflict, that is in helping him tolerate, become aware of and understand the implications of his sexual desires and his aggressive feelings and fantasies.

Self psychology, in contrast, views a considerable aspect of psychopathology as a manifestation of a deficit in maturation, that is a lack of development in some significant areas of functioning, secondary to a failure on the part of the parents to provide the appropriate conditions for emotional growth. This deficit consists of an inability to cope adequately in many situations, for example, to maintain self esteem in the face of narcissistic blows or to be realistic about one's expectations. JUST AS SCHOLARS HAVE STRESSED the important difference between oral and written literature, we must give due attention to dreams in terms of the way of being delivered, i.e., by writing or viva voce. When dealing with orally delivered dreams, we sometimes come upon, unexpectedly, a peculiar type of dream elaboration which has hitherto escaped focused consideration and which I have judged significant enough to become the topic of this essay. At the outset, however, we encounter in our path a major terminological difficulty and we shall facilitate our progress if we clear it up first. Basing himself on a thorough collection of references to dream elaboration in the Freudian canon, Breznitz (1971) shows that Freud was inconsistent in chronologically situating secondary revision during dream-work, after the dream-work proper, and after awakening. To these three moments Breznitz assigns three different labels, viz., primary, secondary and tertiary revision respectively. He concludes (p. 412) that PR is chiefly a primary-process operation; TR is conceivable "mainly" as secondary process (though on p. 411 he states that TR is using "only" secondary-process type of thought): and SR is a mixture of primary and secondary process. Introduction

PIONEERS IN PSYCHOANALYSIS, AS IN ANY FIELD of scientific inquiry, are few and far between. In fact our science may still be too young for us to determine who the significant leaders are since it is often only in retrospect that one can assess the meaningful contributions in the history of a science. So many of the seemingly great chemists and physicists of their time have faded into obscurity that it will be little surprise to our future historians to note that the many, to us, meaningful figures of today will have contributed little of lasting significance to our science of psychoanalysis. Erich Fromm was undoubtedly a pioneer and only the future will reveal if his contributions will continue to take hold on our minds as the edges of psychoanalysis are further explored. This essay will be directed toward examining some facets of the reception of new ideas before history can make a more reasonable assessment.

One of the very great difficulties in the establishment of new ideas in the field of psychoanalysis, perhaps moreso than in other scientific pursuits such as physics and mathematics is the heritage of our ideas from one man, Sigmund Freud, and a form of trusteeship of his ideas that seems to carry on from generation to generation. Trustees are usually assigned the role of guardianship and at times they feel a necessity to decide issues of truth or falsehood in terms of the reigning ideas. I have been particularly interested recently in the impact of the new ideas of self psychology on the overall field of psychoanalysis, and I have often been struck by the wave of responses which these new ideas have evoked. Although some of these responses are quite challenging and provocative, a number of them seem to fail to meet the minimum demands for scientific theory and inquiry. THE QUESTION OF WHAT COMPRISES PSYCHOANALYTIC training—how to best teach a candidate how to become an analyst—has had a long and checkered history. Much has been written over the last seventy years. It is apparent that major shifts have occurred in the definition of supervision, the model for learning in supervision, the use of the analytic versus the didactic teaching method between student and supervisor, and how the supervisor uses himself with his student. These issues remain central and unresolved. I believe they reflect current changes in our understanding of how the analyst can best use himself with his patient. Concepts such as Langs's bi-personal field (1976) and Sullivan's participant-observation (1954) come to mind.

Perhaps a brief overview of the history of supervision is in order. Before psychoanalytic training was formalized, the model was that of master-apprentice. "In the early days, small groups that gathered around Freud analyzed, taught and supervised each other." (Gustin 1958, p. 63) One's personal analysis was seen as the foundation of the future analyst's training (Eckstein and Wallerstein 1958).

In 1922, formal standards were set, along with course work and one's own psychoanalysis, by the International Psycho-Analytic Society which called for the treatment of several patients under supervision (Eckstein and Wallerstein 1958).

In the 1930's there was considerable debate as to how supervision could best be accomplished. One group, from Budapest, believed that supervision—called "control analysis"—was a continuation of the candidate's personal analysis and therefore both should be done by the same analyst.

FIRST I SHALL GIVE THREE STATEMENTS by three patients on the same Monday. A young man in his mid-twenties started his session by saying: "I am feeling very anxious because I am meeting the parents of my girlfriend for the first time tonight." The second patient, a businessman in his late forties, started by saying: "The deal went through successfully last Friday and we have been celebrating it all weekend, yet I feel depressed today." The third patient, a woman in her late thirties, arrived, lay down, and was silent for some twenty minutes. I sensed she had started to cry quietly. Eventually she said: "I am in pain and I do not know why. My children came from school last Friday, and they have done so well the last term that we all went out and enjoyed yourselves. IN FREUD'S EARLY EMPHASIS on the economy of drives and drive derivatives, cast within the frame of reference provided by the libido theory, he put the emphasis on the biologically-derived instinctual components. In the instinctual equation based on elements of pressure, aim, source and object, Freud's emphasis fell on the elements of pressure, aim and source, while the role of the object was relatively minimized. As Freud (1915) observed:

The object of an instinct is the thing in regard to which or through which the instinct is able to achieve its aim. It is what is most variable about an instinct and is not originally connected with it, but becomes assigned to it only in consequence of being peculiarly fitted to make satisfaction possible. (p. 122)

In the ensuing three score and more years, the analytic view of the role of the object and its place in psychological functioning has undergone a radical revision. Under the stimulus provided by the object relations theorists, analysts have come to regard the impact of significant objects and the child's interaction with significant objects during the course of development as some of the most significant and central dimensions of the psychoanalytic perspective. We now recognize that the development of drives and drive derivatives in the human individual is inherently connected with and powerfully influenced by the quality of ongoing relationships that the developing individual experiences with the important objects in his life experience. The context of object relationships determines not only the patterning of the expression of drives and their derivatives, but also powerfully influences other important dimensions of the individual's developing ego, superego and self-organization.

FEW PREDICAMENTS ARE SO HEARTBREAKING as that of the teen-ager whose world seems shattered and who is inconsolable in his grief. His distress has been touched off by some very real, very acutely felt loss—loss of a loved one, loss of self-esteem, loss of a dream, even loss of an image he had had of himself (Toolan 1978); (Ostrov and Offer 1978). Sustenance seems gone. Life appears bleak. Helplessness has replaced what had been enthusiasm about his present and optimism about his future. As real as they are, these phases are often short-lived (Turns 1978). Growth, in body and experience, is extraordinarily rapid, and highs and lows tumble over one another as the young person adjusts to the changes.

As adults we sometimes paint a bitter-sweet, oversentimentalized picture of adolescence, remembering its excitement, forgetting some of its pain. So we tend to minimize the severity of the turbulence in the adolescent we know. With bemused paternalism we characterize his moody swings as cute or over-wrought, we use platitudes to euphemize his felt despair, or we substitute sympathy for empathy because we don't want to experience his anguish.

We are all familiar with the television version of the post-pubertal boy or girl whose gropings are exaggerated into histrionic, pseudo-adult posturing, which peers greet with strident solicitude, and adults with self-righteous and patronizing banalities, false good cheer, and sly, knowing looks. The stereotype may work in a situation comedy, but there is more to real adolescent depression than this. Suicides and the suicide rate have accelerated among the 15 to 24 year olds in the last two decades (Petzel and Cline 1978).

THE PURPOSE OF THIS PAPER is to clarify and consolidate some of the major concepts used in assessing clinical appropriateness for psychoanalysis. This paper is not so much a description of how to assess analyzability as it is a description of some psychological and environmental concepts and processes that interact in order for a patient to be analyzable or unanalyzable. If we have a thorough understanding of the various psychological and environmental factors that interact in order to make a patient analyzable or unanalyzable then the degree of analyzability at times may become readily apparent in the initial assessment sessions where at other times it cannot be pre-analytically assessed, i.e., it cannot be properly assessed until the patient has been in treatment for a significant amount of time. For the purpose of this paper, analyzability can be defined as a state of readiness that involves the capacity to cognitively and emotionally understand psychoanalysis plus the capacity for constructive psychological and behavioral change as a result of that understanding.

Most analysts would agree that the judgement of analyzability is often subjectively made. Many of these intuitively made judgements are most satisfying and have confirmed the wisdom of empathic intuition. Although we must remain respectful of empathic intuition, the assessment of analyzability is far too important a decision in the life of the patient to be made by the unreliable forces of intuition. It should instead be made with a cognitive and rational understanding of the relevant concepts at this stage of our knowledge. This knowledge may reveal that psychoanalysis is contraindicated and even dangerous to a specific patient's mental and physical well being.

This paper consists of revised and abbreviated versions of discussions that appear in: Paolino, T.J.Jr. (1981).

THIS ISSUE OF CONTEMPORARY PSYCHOANALYSIS is dedicated to the memory of Max Deutscher (1916-1979), teacher, supervisor, analyst and colleague, as well as a founding editor of this journal. In addition to several pieces by and about Max, we have decided to commemorate his memory by publishing a series of invited articles concerning object relations theories.1 Max taught the course at the William Alanson White Institute on object relations theory, and it occupied a central place in his theoretical and clinical concerns. We feel that the best way to express our appreciation for Max's intellectual curiosity, personal enthusiasm, and dedication to psychoanalysis, both theoretical and technical, is to help to clarify and articulate important issues within this major area of contemporary psychoanalytic thought.

THIS PAPER WAS READ at the March 13, 1962 meeting of the Association of Psychoanalytic Psychologists. Dr. Rose Spiegel was the discussant. Although Max intended to complete it for publication, it was found among his papers in less than final form. It is published here with minor editorial changes.

Of the several unfinished manuscripts that Max left behind—on anniversary reactions, on work, on neutrality, on post-partum psychopathology, this paper on fathering stands out. In those who were susceptible, he inspired an enduring respect, love and loyalty. He was a gifted teacher.

In addition to providing us with a vivid memory of Max's unique expression and observation, this paper has a substantive importance.

ALTHOUGH THE DELINEATION OF splitting-and-idealization as an essential step in early development found its place in Melanie Klein's theories of development quite soon in her researches, it was only with the 1946 paper "A Note on Some Schizoid Mechanisms" that the wide variety of splitting processes, normal and pathological, came under systematic scrutiny. The use of splitting processes in the sense of constructive differentiation as against their use for breaking links in the service of defense found repeated expression in the literature of the 50's and 60's. But Wilfred Bion's description of processes of attention and their relation to thinking in "Attention and Interpretation" marked the beginning of a new dimension of investigation of the modes of operation of splitting processes. Those who had followed Mrs. Klein's way of thinking, her implicit model of the mind, that is, assumed that splitting processes operated by unconscious phantasy, implemented by omnipotence, effecting concrete alterations in the structure of self and objects in psychic reality. Bion's extension of Kleinian mechanisms to an arena of operation on mental functions as well as mental structures revealed a new level of phenomenology in the consulting room.

This paper is intended merely as an illustration of how these two levels of splitting processes can operate in parallel and potentiate one another's impact on mental states. The exposition will be confined to a single piece of rather intricate clinical material for which a considerable amount of background in the psychoanalytical process is required to consolidate the credibility of the interpretation being put forward.

MANY YEARS AGO, BEFORE I BECAME a psychologist and a psychoanalyst, when I was about to leave for Vienna for training in these fields, I went to bid good-bye to Jessie Taft who had been my professor at the Pennsylvania School of Social Work. She had been analyzed by Otto Rank, was profoundly influenced by his thinking and was later to become his translator. She was not happy about my going to the Freudian-oriented Vienna Institute for Psychoanalysis, and she said: "In my opinion Rank was as far ahead of Freud as Freud was of the hypnotists." This did not deter me. In fact, I did not understand it. I put it down to the bias against Freudian psychology which was so prevalent in academic and professional circles at that time. It was only many years later that I came to understand the full significance of the remark.

Otto Rank was indeed way ahead of his time. But what do we mean by that, and what is its importance? From our current vantage point it must mean that his imagination, inventiveness and creativity led him to conclusions that we in our time hold to be true and valid, but which were not accepted in his time. But this is certainly equally true of Freud, or of any great, original thinker whose insights stretch beyond the accepted knowledge of his time. What is particularly unique about Rank, however, is that he perceived the relativity of truth; he understood that the interpretation of the psychology of man is dependent upon the frame of reference, the paradigm, the way of thinking of the historical time and place in which a psychological theory is formulated.
